passage:
"So, which class now, Maria?" asked Papa's cousin Zainab, passing the plate of pakoras.
"Fifth."
"And how are the marks?"
"Fine."
"Do you like your teacher?"
"Yes."
Maria stared at the plate. The questions felt like a queue at a counter.
Zainab tried again. "I saw a kite on the roof when I came in. Yours?"
"Yes!" Maria looked up. "It's a fighter kite, red and yellow. Papa built the frame." A giggle. "The tail was mine. It has ten knots."
"Show me after lunch?"
"Yes, come!"

qa.q: What class is Maria in?
qa.a: Fifth.

qa.q: What did the questions about class and marks feel like to Maria?
qa.a: Like a queue at a counter. Maria gave one-word answers and stared at the plate, which suggests boredom and a bit of pressure.

qa.q: What could Zainab try next time to help a child relax?
qa.a: Ask about something the child enjoys, as Zainab did with the kite question, rather than another question about class or marks.

qa.q: How might Zainab feel when Maria suddenly lights up about the kite?
qa.a: Pleased and relieved that the conversation finally opened. Zainab changed the question, and Maria answered with energy and invited Zainab to see it.

grounding: A child at a relatives' gathering gives one-word answers to questions about class and marks, then relaxes when asked about a hobby.

passage: My name is Charu. At Nani's birthday lunch, my Masi Jaya sat next to me and said, "Which class? Marks good?" I said, "Sixth. Yes." She asked what the teacher's name was. I said, "Mrs Iyer." I kept looking at my glass and hoping the questions would end. It felt like a test I hadn't studied for. Then Masi said, "Nani told me you draw comics. Is that true?" I sat up. "Yes! A superhero who is afraid of the dark." Masi laughed and asked what the hero's name is. I talked all through dessert. I remember it as the moment I stopped counting the minutes.

qa.q: Whose birthday lunch was Charu at?
qa.a: Nani's.

qa.q: How did Charu feel about the questions on class and marks?
qa.a: Uncomfortable and eager for them to end. Charu kept looking at the glass and said it felt like a test not studied for.

qa.q: What turned the conversation around for Charu?
qa.a: Masi Jaya asked about Charu's comics, something Nani had mentioned, so Charu could talk about something Charu cared about.

qa.q: How might Masi Jaya feel after hearing about the superhero afraid of the dark?
qa.a: Interested and glad she found a topic that works. Masi laughed and asked more, which kept Charu talking all through dessert.

grounding: A child at a relatives' lunch gets class and marks questions, answers briefly, and relaxes when asked about a hobby.

passage:
"Preeti beta, which class now?" said the aunty in the green sari.
"Five."
"And marks?"
"Good."
"How good? Ninety?"
"Eighty-something."
"Hmm. Study more." The aunty moved on. Another uncle took her place.
"Preeti! Which class?"
"Five."
"Marks?"
"Fine."
Preeti stared at the carpet. Then her cousin Samir, sixteen, flopped onto the sofa beside her. "Hey. Are you still drawing those comic strips about the cat detective?"
Preeti's head came up. "Yes! He solved a new case. The stolen fish." She pulled out a notebook. "Want to see?"
"Obviously."
For the next twenty minutes, Preeti talked nonstop.

qa.q: What was Preeti's comic strip about?
qa.a: A cat detective.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel during the questions about class and marks?
qa.a: She felt bored and uncomfortable, giving one-word answers and staring at the carpet.

qa.q: What did Samir do differently that helped Preeti open up?
qa.a: He asked about her comic strips, a hobby she loves, instead of marks, and she relaxed and talked nonstop.

qa.q: How might the aunty in the green sari see Preeti?
qa.a: She may have thought Preeti was quiet or shy, not realising her questions felt like an interview.

grounding: Shows a child giving one-word answers to adults' repeated questions about class and marks, then relaxing when asked about a hobby.

passage:
Diwali at Dadi's house is always full of relatives. This year I counted: eleven people asked me which class I was in, and nine asked my marks. By the tenth "Beta, which class?" I was answering with one word and looking at my shoes. It felt like an interview I hadn't prepared for.
Then Yamini aunty sat down next to me with a plate of kaju katli. She didn't ask about school. She said, "Akash, your mother says you collect cricket cards. Who's your rarest?"
I nearly dropped my sweet. I ran to get my folder. I showed her the whole thing, the shiny ones, the old ones, the one I traded three cards for. She asked questions about every page.
That was the best part of Diwali. I'm going to show her my new ones next year.

qa.q: How many people asked Akash's marks?
qa.a: Nine asked about marks.

qa.q: How did Akash feel by the tenth 'Beta, which class?'
qa.a: Akash felt tired and uncomfortable, as if in an interview, answering in one word and looking at the shoes.

qa.q: What did Yamini aunty do that made Akash relax?
qa.a: She asked about the cricket card collection instead of school, which let Akash share something loved.

qa.q: How might Yamini aunty have felt looking at the folder?
qa.a: She seemed interested and pleased, asking questions about every page.

grounding: Shows a child at a relatives' gathering giving one-word answers to questions about class and marks, then relaxing when asked about a hobby.

passage:
Note to self after Sunday's family lunch.
Lalit (9) arrived with his parents and was passed from relative to relative. I heard "Which class?" at least six times, and "How much did you get in maths?" four. He answered each with one word. By the time the rice came, he was sitting on the stairs alone, poking a crack in the step.
I remembered his mother saying he'd started keeping silkworms for a school project. So I sat down beside him and asked, "How are the silkworms? Have any made cocoons yet?"
He looked up. "Three! And one is really fat." He talked for fifteen minutes about leaves and cocoons.
Next time we host, I'll tell the relatives to ask him about the silkworms.
Nandini

qa.q: How many silkworms had made cocoons?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling as he sat alone on the stairs?
qa.a: He seemed bored and worn out, tired of answering the same questions about class and marks.

qa.q: What did Nandini plan for next time, and why is it helpful?
qa.a: Nandini planned to tell relatives to ask Lalit about the silkworms, since a hobby question helps him relax and talk.

qa.q: How might Lalit's parents see the change in him?
qa.a: They would probably be pleased to see him chatting happily instead of sitting alone on the stairs.

grounding: Shows a child giving one-word answers to adults' repeated questions about school and relaxing when asked about a hobby.

passage:
Saturday night
Sarika's diary. Cousin's engagement today. I counted: nine people asked me "Which class now?" and seven asked "How many marks?" I said "Six" and "Okay" and "Fine" about a hundred times. My face got tired from smiling. Then Sabina Phuppo sat next to me with her plate and said, "I heard you're drawing comics now. What's the story about?" I told her about Captain Pickle for twenty minutes. She laughed at the part where he falls into the chutney jar. She even asked what happens next. I forgot I was at a party. I'm drawing her into the next chapter as the queen.

qa.q: How many people asked Sarika about marks?
qa.a: Seven people asked about marks.

qa.q: How did Sarika feel answering "Which class now?" again and again?
qa.a: Sarika felt bored and awkward, giving one-word answers until even smiling felt tiring 😅

qa.q: What could other relatives ask Sarika next time?
qa.a: They could ask about something Sarika enjoys, like the comics, instead of class and marks.

qa.q: What might Sabina Phuppo have enjoyed about the talk?
qa.a: She probably enjoyed seeing Sarika light up and laughing at the chutney jar part, a real conversation instead of an interview.

grounding: Shows a child at a family function giving one-word answers to class-and-marks questions, then relaxing when asked about a hobby.
